name: APT38
summary: APT38 is a North Korean state-sponsored threat group that specializes in financial cyber operations; it has been attributed to the Reconnaissance General Bureau. Active since at least 2014, APT38 has targeted banks, financial institutions, casinos, cryptocurrency exchanges, SWIFT system endpoints, and ATMs in at least 38 countries worldwide. Significant operations include the 2016 Bank of Bangladesh heist, during which APT38 stole $81 million, as well as attacks against Bancomext and Banco de Chile; some of their attacks have been destructive. North Korean group definitions are known to have significant overlap, and some security researchers report all North Korean state-sponsored cyber activity under the name Lazarus Group instead of tracking clusters or subgroups.

procedures.text: APT38 has created fake domains to imitate legitimate venture capital or bank domains.
APT38 has obtained and used open-source tools such as Mimikatz.
APT38 has conducted watering holes schemes to gain initial access to victims.
APT38 has conducted spearphishing campaigns using malicious email attachments.
APT38 has used a command-line tunneler, NACHOCHEESE, to give them shell access to a victim’s machine. Additionally, APT38 has used batch scripts.
APT38 has created new services or modified existing ones to run executables, commands, or scripts.
APT38 has used the Windows API to execute code within a victim's system.
APT38 has used cron to create pre-scheduled and periodic background jobs on a Linux system.

APT38 has used Task Scheduler to run programs at system startup or on a scheduled basis for persistence. Additionally, APT38 has used living-off-the-land scripts to execute a malicious script via a scheduled task.
APT38 has used PowerShell to execute commands and other operational tasks.
APT38 has used VBScript to execute commands and other operational tasks.
APT38 has used links to execute a malicious Visual Basic script.
APT38 has attempted to lure victims into enabling malicious macros within email attachments. Additionally, APT38 has used malicious Word documents and shortcut files.
HOPLIGHT: HOPLIGHT has used WMI to recompile the Managed Object Format (MOF) files in the WMI repository.
DarkComet: DarkComet can execute various types of scripts on the victim’s machine.
KillDisk: KillDisk loads and executes functions from a DLL.
APT38 uses a tool called CLEANTOAD that has the capability to modify Registry keys.
APT38 has used web shells for persistence or to ensure redundant access.
APT38 has installed a new Windows service to establish persistence.

Mimikatz: The Mimikatz credential dumper has been extended to include Skeleton Key domain controller authentication bypass functionality. The `LSADUMP::ChangeNTLM` and `LSADUMP::SetNTLM` modules can also manipulate the password hash of an account without knowing the clear text value.
Net: The `net localgroup` and `net group` commands in Net can be used to add existing users to local and domain groups.
Net: The `net user username \password` commands in Net can be used to create a local account.
Net: The `net user username \password \domain` commands in Net can be used to create a domain account.
HOPLIGHT: HOPLIGHT can use WMI event subscriptions to create persistence.
DarkComet: DarkComet adds several Registry entries to enable automatic execution at every system startup.
Mimikatz: The Mimikatz credential dumper contains an implementation of an SSP.
APT38 has injected malicious payloads into the `explorer.exe` process.
APT38 has used the legitimate application `ieinstal.exe` to bypass UAC.

KillDisk: KillDisk has attempted to get the access token of a process by calling `OpenProcessToken`. If KillDisk gets the access token, then it attempt to modify the token privileges with `AdjustTokenPrivileges`.

Mimikatz: Mimikatz's `MISC::AddSid` module can append any SID or user/group account to a user's SID-History. Mimikatz also utilizes SID-History Injection to expand the scope of other components such as generated Kerberos Golden Tickets and DCSync beyond a single domain.

APT38 has used a utility called CLOSESHAVE that can securely delete a file from the system. They have also removed malware, tools, or other non-native files used during the intrusion to reduce their footprint or as part of the post-intrusion cleanup process.
APT38 has used several code packing methods such as Themida, Enigma, VMProtect, and Obsidium, to pack their implants.
ECCENTRICBANDWAGON: ECCENTRICBANDWAGON has encrypted strings with RC4.
APT38 has renamed system utilities, such as `rundll32.exe` and `mshta.exe`, to avoid detection.
APT38 has put several spaces before a file extension to avoid detection and suspicion.
APT38 has modified data timestamps to mimic files that are in the same folder on a compromised host.
APT38 has used the RC4 algorithm to decrypt configuration data.
APT38 has used CHM files to move concealed payloads.

procedures.text: APT38 has used a renamed version of `mshta.exe` to execute malicious HTML files.
APT38 has used `msiexec.exe` to execute malicious files.
APT38 has used rundll32.exe to execute binaries, scripts, and Control Panel Item files and to execute code via proxy to avoid triggering security tools.
APT38 has created a mutex to avoid duplicate execution.
KillDisk: KillDisk registers as a service under the Plug-And-Play Support name.
DarkComet: DarkComet has dropped itself onto victim machines with file names such as WinDefender.Exe and winupdate.exe in an apparent attempt to masquerade as a legitimate file.
Net: The `net use \\system\share /delete` command can be used in Net to remove an established connection to a network share.
KillDisk: KillDisk deletes application, security, setup, and system event logs from Windows systems.
APT38 has unhooked DLLs to disable endpoint detection and response (EDR) or anti-virus (AV) tools.
APT38 clears Window Event logs and Sysmon logs from the system.
APT38 have created firewall exemptions on specific ports, including ports 443, 6443, 8443, and 9443.
APT38 has used ISO and VHD files to deploy malware and to bypass Mark-of-the-Web (MOTW) security measures.
APT38 have created firewall exemptions on specific ports, including ports 443, 6443, 8443, and 9443.
APT38 has prepended a space to all of their terminal commands to operate without leaving traces in the HISTCONTROL environment.
Mimikatz: Mimikatz’s `LSADUMP::DCShadow` module can be used to make AD updates by temporarily setting a computer to be a DC.
DarkComet: DarkComet can disable Security Center functions like the Windows Firewall.
APT38 used a Trojan called KEYLIME to capture keystrokes from the victim’s machine.
HOPLIGHT: HOPLIGHT has the capability to harvest credentials and passwords from the SAM database.
APT38 has used brute force techniques to attempt account access when passwords are unknown or when password hashes are unavailable.

Mimikatz: Mimikatz performs credential dumping to obtain account and password information useful in gaining access to additional systems and enterprise network resources. It contains functionality to acquire information about credentials in many ways, including from the LSASS Memory.

procedures.text: Mimikatz: Mimikatz contains functionality to acquire credentials from the Windows Credential Manager.
Mimikatz: Mimikatz's kerberos module can create golden tickets.
Mimikatz: Mimikatz's kerberos module can create silver tickets.
Mimikatz: Mimikatz's `CRYPTO` module can create and export various types of authentication certificates.
APT38 leveraged Sysmon to understand the processes, services in the organization.
APT38 has attempted to get detailed information about a compromised host, including the operating system, version, patches, hotfixes, and service packs.
APT38 have enumerated files and directories, or searched in specific locations within a compromised host.
APT38 has identified primary users, currently logged in users, sets of users that commonly use a system, or inactive users.
APT38 installed a port monitoring tool, MAPMAKER, to print the active TCP connections on the local system.
APT38 has enumerated network shares on a compromised host.
Net: The `net time` command can be used in Net to determine the local or remote system time.
APT38 has collected browser bookmark information to learn more about compromised hosts, obtain personal information about users, and acquire details about internal network resources.
APT38 has identified security software, configurations, defensive tools, and sensors installed on a compromised system.
HOPLIGHT: HOPLIGHT has been observed collecting victim machine volume information.
Net: The `net start` command can be used in Net to find information about Windows services.
HOPLIGHT: A variant of HOPLIGHT hooks lsass.exe, and lsass.exe then checks the Registry for the data value 'rdpproto' under the key `SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa Name`.
Net: Commands such as `net view` can be used in Net to gather information about available remote systems.
Net: Commands such as `net group` and `net localgroup` can be used in Net to gather information about and manipulate groups.
Net: Commands such as `net group /domain` can be used in Net to gather information about and manipulate groups.
Net: Commands under `net user` can be used in Net to gather information about and manipulate user accounts.
Net: Net commands used with the `/domain` flag can be used to gather information about and manipulate user accounts on the current domain.
Net: The `net accounts` and `net accounts /domain` commands with Net can be used to obtain password policy information.
HOPLIGHT: HOPLIGHT can enumerate device drivers located in the registry at `HKLM\Software\WBEM\WDM`.
HOPLIGHT: HOPLIGHT has been observed loading several APIs associated with Pass the Hash.
DarkComet: DarkComet can open an active screen of the victim’s machine and take control of the mouse and keyboard.
Net: Lateral movement can be done with Net through `net use` commands to connect to the on remote systems.
Mimikatz: Mimikatz’s `LSADUMP::DCSync` and `KERBEROS::PTT` modules implement the three steps required to extract the krbtgt account hash and create/use Kerberos tickets.
APT38 used a Trojan called KEYLIME to collect data from the clipboard.
APT38 has collected data from a compromised host.
ECCENTRICBANDWAGON: ECCENTRICBANDWAGON has stored keystrokes and screenshots within the `%temp%\GoogleChrome`, `%temp%\Downloads`, and `%temp%\TrendMicroUpdate` directories.
ECCENTRICBANDWAGON: ECCENTRICBANDWAGON can capture screenshots and store them locally.
DarkComet: DarkComet can listen in to victims' conversations through the system’s microphone.
DarkComet: DarkComet can access the victim’s webcam to take pictures.
APT38 used a backdoor, NESTEGG, that has the capability to download and upload files to and from a victim’s machine. Additionally, APT38 has downloaded other payloads onto a victim’s machine.
APT38 used a backdoor, QUICKRIDE, to communicate to the C2 server over HTTP and HTTPS.
HOPLIGHT: HOPLIGHT has multiple C2 channels in place in case one fails.
HOPLIGHT: HOPLIGHT has multiple proxy options that mask traffic between the malware and the remote operators.
HOPLIGHT: HOPLIGHT has utilized Zlib compression to obfuscate the communications payload.
HOPLIGHT: HOPLIGHT has connected outbound over TCP port 443 with a FakeTLS method.
HOPLIGHT: HOPLIGHT has used its C2 channel to exfiltrate data.
KillDisk: KillDisk is able to delete system files to make the system unbootable and targets 35 different types of files for deletion.
KillDisk: KillDisk looks for and terminates two non-standard processes, one of which is an ICS application.
APT38 has used a custom secure delete function to make deleted files unrecoverable.
APT38 has used Hermes ransomware to encrypt files with AES256.
APT38 has used a custom MBR wiper named BOOTWRECK, which will initiate a system reboot after wiping the victim's MBR.
APT38 has used a custom MBR wiper named BOOTWRECK to render systems inoperable.
APT38 has used DYEPACK to create, delete, and alter records in databases used for SWIFT transactions.
APT38 has used DYEPACK to manipulate SWIFT messages en route to a printer.
APT38 has used DYEPACK.FOX to manipulate PDF data as it is accessed to remove traces of fraudulent SWIFT transactions from the data displayed to the end user.
KillDisk: KillDisk erases the master boot record (MBR) and system logs, leaving the system unusable.
KillDisk: KillDisk terminates various processes to get the user to reboot the victim machine.
